newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says 500 rebels killed in Kikwit battle.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says 500 rebels killed in Kikwit battle.

text.p: Zaire said on Tuesday government forces were battling to retake the western town of Kikwit and had killed several hundred rebels.
Independent sources confirmed a belated counter-offensive after months of retreat from Laurent Kabila's rebels but said the clashes were near Kenge, far to the west of Kikwit.

"We are in the process of retaking Kikwit. Intense fighting is taking place. The rebels have lost 500 men," Prime Minister Likulia Bolongo's military adviser, Captain Aime Atembina, told a news conference in the capital Kinshasa.
He did not say when the fighting started and added that Kikwit, more than 400 km (250 miles) east of Kinshasa, had never been completely taken by the rebels who announced its capture over a week ago.
Sources in touch with the city, including diplomats, have described it as firmly in rebel control and the rear base for an imminent push to capture the capital.

Diplomatic sources could not confirm any fighting near Kikwit where the rebels have been airlifting large numbers of reinforcements. Residents in radio contact with Kinshasa said the town of 160,000 people was calm on Tuesday with a heavy rebel presence.

However, they confirmed that a counter-offensive involving about 3,000 soldiers loyal to President Mobutu Sese Seko had been launched around Kenge about 200 km (125 miles) to the west of Kikwit. "They are more or less in control of Kenge," one diplomat said. Residents said there were many dead on both sides in the fighting at Kenge, 250 km (160 miles) east of Kinshasa.
A war of disinformation is picking up pace with rebel officials laughing in their headquarters in Lubumbashi at government's claims to be poised to retake Kikwit.

In Kinshasa the government and diplomats dismissed rebel claims to be only 60 km (40 miles) away from the city's international airport as ridiculous. Travellers coming to Kinshasa from the east also said they had seen no sign of the rebels.

The report of at least a limited fightback by Zaire's ragged army came as the presidency announced Mobutu would fly to neighbouring Gabon on Wednesday to meet the presidents of five former French African colonies and Equatorial Guinea.
Presidential aides said Mobutu was not fleeing the country and would return by Friday after talks on the crisis. The official communique did not specify when he would return.
Atembina said government troops, who have lost control of most of Zaire's territory to rebels since October, would fight to prevent guerrilla leader Kabila entering Kinshasa by force.
He denied suggestions that foreign allies might be fighting alongside the Zaire army in their bid to push the rebels back.
"The only foreign troops are fighting against the FAZ (Zaire army)," he said.
There are persistent reports that Mobutu ally Jonas Savimbi, leader of the UNITA movement in neighbouring Angola, has sent men to help Zaire's embattled president.
Following last Sunday's failed talks between Mobutu and Kabila, fear and apprehension are increasingly gripping inhabitants of the capital.

In the city's teeming suburbs many residents say they have nothing to fear from the rebels. However, they do fear the prospect of panic and desperation amongst soldiers of the defeated army should Kabila's rebel alliance take the fight to topple Mobutu to the capital.
United Nations agencies stepped up security precautions in Kinhsasa on Tuesday, evacuating the last handful of non-essential staff, a senior U.N. source said.
"We are sending away non-essential staff. It will involve the departure of about five people, leaving about 15 people in Kinshasa," the source told Reuters.

The U.N. source said those remaining were heads of United Nations agencies and a few key staff. Tuesday's decision became automatic when the United Nations raised its security level to phase four. The highest level -- phase five -- is complete evacuation, he said.
Asked why the move became necessary, the source said: "In the U.N. the more they (rebels) approach the more we have a tendency to leave as a precaution."
More than 3,000 American, Belgian, French and British troops are stationed in Central Africa ready to evacuate foreigners.
There was no indication that the U.N. move would trigger the evacuation. More than 1,500 Belgians are the largest group of Europeans and North Americans in Kinshasa.
